title: Names and Numbers
about: How website names get turned into the numbers computers use.

cards.prompt:
[[Routers|router]] deliver [[packets|packet]] by [[IP address|ip-address]], like `198.51.100.10`, not by name.

So why do websites have names?

options.text: Routers need numbers, but people remember names
Names make packets travel faster than numbers
options.nudge: A name doesn't change a packet's speed: who finds names easier, people or routers?

options.text: Names hide a website's IP address from hackers
options.nudge: Anyone can look up a site's address, so names hide nothing: who finds them easier?

options.text: Names let you skip the routers and go straight there
options.nudge: Every packet still goes through routers, which only read addresses: so who are names for?

cards.explanation: Routers deliver packets by **IP address**; names are for people, since `example.com` is easier to remember than `198.51.100.10`. So something has to turn the name into an address first.
cards.hint: Who uses names, and what do routers need to deliver a packet?

cards.title: The internet's contacts app
cards.body:
A contacts app turns a **name** into a **number**. The internet has the same thing: the **Domain Name System**, or **DNS**.

Give it a name like `example.com`, and it gives back an [[IP address]] like `198.51.100.10`. That's a **DNS lookup**, and it happens before almost every connection.

cards.prompt: Match each part of the contacts app to its internet version.
cards.explanation: People use the **name**, the network uses the **number** (IP address), and **DNS** looks one up from the other. With the address, your device connects, like a phone dialling.
cards.hint: People remember the name, the [[network]] uses the number, and something looks one up from the other.
cards.nudge: Line them up by job: what you remember, what the network uses, the look-up, and the step after.

cards.prompt: Run `nslookup example.com` to ask [[DNS]] for example.com's address.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Ask DNS for the address of example.com
commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 198.51.100.10
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

cards.explanation: DNS gave **two** addresses: [[IPv4]] `198.51.100.10` and [[IPv6]] `2001:db8::10`, and either works. The `Server` and `Address` lines at the top are the DNS helper that answered, not example.com.
cards.hint: Type the [[command]] exactly as it's shown, then press Enter.
cards.nudge: Check the spelling and the space: the tool's name first, then the website's.

cards.prompt:
In `mail.example.org`, `mail` is a **subdomain** the owner added, `org` is the **top-level domain** (**TLD**), shared by millions, and `example` is the registered **domain**.

Names read right to left: order the parts, **most general** first.
cards.explanation: Right to left: the TLD `org`, shared by millions; then `example`, making the registered `example.org`; then `mail`, a subdomain its owner added.
cards.hint: Start at the right-hand end: which part is shared by the most names?
cards.nudge: Reading left to right gives the most specific part first: flip it.

cards.prompt: A domain's owner can add any subdomains to its **left**. Who controls `login.example.com.example.org`?

options.nudge: That's in the middle, not at the end: what matters is the registered domain on the right.

options.text: Both owners share control of it
options.nudge: Only one domain is registered here: read from the right to find it.
The leftmost part is a subdomain the owner chose: look at the right-hand end instead.

cards.explanation: From the right, the registered domain is `example.org`, so `login.example.com` is just a subdomain **its owner** added. Scammers use this trick to make links *look* like another site's.
cards.hint: Read from the right: find the [[TLD]], then the domain next to it; the rest is a [[subdomain]].

cards.prompt:
Many UK names end in `.co.uk`: the TLD is `uk`, and `co.uk` is shared by millions of companies, like `.com`.

Who controls `shop.example.co.uk`?

options.text: Whoever runs co.uk, since it sits next to the TLD
options.nudge: `co.uk` is shared by millions, like `.com`: look one step further left.

options.text: The UK government, because it ends in uk
options.nudge: A country code shows where a name is registered, not who runs the site.

options.text: Whoever owns the shop part at the start
options.nudge: The leftmost part is a subdomain: its owner is whoever registered the domain to its right.

cards.explanation: From the right, `uk` is the TLD and `co.uk` a shared ending, like `.com`. So `example.co.uk` is the registered domain, and **its owner** controls `shop.example.co.uk`.
cards.hint: Use the right-to-left rule: which part would one company actually register?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **DNS** turns names into [[IP addresses|ip-address]], like a contacts app.
- Names are read **right to left**: TLD, domain, then subdomains.
- A domain's owner controls every subdomain to its left.
